speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in light of the announcement yesterday with respect to the reduction in government expenditures this year and next, I am sure that all members of the House would want to be sure in some ongoing way that these reductions and expenditures would not inconvenience those who are least able to protect themselves, particularly those living in the disadvantaged regions of the country. Therefore, I hope this motion will find general acceptance. Under the provisions of Standing Order 43 I move, seconded by the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. MacLean):
That the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion be instructed by the House to monitor and report, on a monthly basis, any detrimental impact which the alteration of government expenditures might have on the present economic and social development in regions in which the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has a responsibility.

speechtext: Before proceeding with oral questions, I know that hon. members will want to join me in recognizing with appropriate warmth the return to the chamber of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale).

subtopic: RECOGNITION OF RETURN TO CHAMBER OF MEMBER FOR BRANDON-SOURIS FOLLOWING ILLNESS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: RECOGNITION OF RETURN TO CHAMBER OF MEMBER FOR BRANDON-SOURIS FOLLOWING ILLNESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may be allowed a few words on this occasion, I have had about four speeches burning in my bosom for the last few weeks. I will not try to unload them all at one time, but I should like to express appreciation, first of all, to you, Sir, for your messages on behalf of all hon. members of this House during my recent illness.
I should like especially to mention messages received from the three leading officials of this chamber. When a person has been through what I have been through in the last few weeks-and I am sure the hon. member for Glen-garry-Prescott-Russell will agree with me in this regard- he thinks about the chamber and the things which are taking place here, and it sort of assumes an ethereal glow. All one can see is the stained glass windows, and reflected in the glow is the halo effect which seems to reside over some figures in the chamber to a greater extent than to others. This was actually substantiated in my own experience because the warmest messages and the messages which showed the greatest concern and personal involvement came from the right hon. Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the right hon. member for Prince Albert. That is why the halo effect is stronger around these three people than any other, in my mind's eye.

December 19, 1975
House of Commons
I first became aware of the Prime Minister at the Resources for Tomorrow Conference back in 1961 when he was then a professor. He has demonstrated many hidden resources since that time since he has assumed the responsibility for the leadership of this House. The Leader of the Opposition wrote a most encouraging and helpful note at a most critical time. The right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert, with his great sense of timing-one hour before I went for surgery-sent to my room an autographed copy of his book "One Canada". Believe me, that was a reality to hang on to for the next few days. I think it was Thomas Carlyle who said that if you want to see demonstrated beyond a shadow of a doubt the truth of original sin, attend a session of the House of Commons. Of course, he was referring to the British house. You might even have it demonstrated here. But let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that there is a warmth and friendship that you find only in this place and I do appreciate everything that has been done and written and said on my behalf.
I should like to extend a special message to the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) who is not with us this morning. He too, made a concrete gesture. He sent me a tape in quadraphonic sound so that the music was coming at me from all sides-and not of an Irish jig but a beautiful tape recording of "The Sound of Music". I was just going to suggest that he make the same gesture to Joe Davidson at this Christmas time because as we all know, music hath charms to soothe the savage breast. A wise man also has said, "Let me write the songs of a nation and I care not who makes its laws."
I should like to mention, too, the staff of the National Defence Medical Centre, one of the finest hospitals in the nation, under the leadership of Dr. Fitzgibbon.

subtopic: RECOGNITION OF RETURN TO CHAMBER OF MEMBER FOR BRANDON-SOURIS FOLLOWING ILLNESS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: RECOGNITION OF RETURN TO CHAMBER OF MEMBER FOR BRANDON-SOURIS FOLLOWING ILLNESS
speechtext:
Also the staff of the Civic hospital under Dr. Keon. It is one of the finest cardiac centres in the nation and it is going to be in the forefront when the new cardiac unit opens some time in the spring.
Perhaps I might be allowed one final message, Mr. Speaker. On the eve of Christmas I recall an old saying: plus ga change, plus c'est la meme chose. The first message I receive when I come back to the House is the decree of Caesar Augustus that all the world should be taxed. It is not simple, it is not new-it is an old message. I am sure it is more than coincidence that it has been saved for the Christmas period; but we know from history that man proposes and God disposes.
I wind up my remarks by extending the greetings of the thousands of Tiny Tims and Bob Cratchets, the backbone of the nation: A Merry Christmas to all and God bless us all-and God help us all.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps at this juncture it might be advantageous if I asked the government House leader his intentions with respect to the business of the House today and perhaps somewhat into the future.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subsubtopic: LEGISLATION TO BE DEALT WITH BEFORE CHRISTMAS RECESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there have been discussions amongst the House leaders about the conclusion of the business before the House pending an adjournment motion being accepted. Perhaps I could begin by saying that the government will require, before the adjournment, the disposition of three bills which are now before the House: Bill C-69, Bill C-77 and Bill C-52. All these measures must come into effect before the end of the year. Therefore, this is the basis upon which we are planning.
Bill C-69 is now at report stage. I believe there is some hope that we might complete the report stage today. At any rate, I think we should be working in that direction. However, before calling Bill C-69, for one consideration

alone apart from any other, that is, the desirability of getting as many bills as possible to the other place so that they can be disposed of before we adjourn, I am calling the report stage of Bill C-77 as the first order of business today. It may be there will be a disposition, also, to give third reading if the debate is not prolonged. I would then call Bill C-69. If we do complete report stage today on Bill C-69, there is, I hope, a unanimous disposition to sit tomorrow to complete all business. These are all very tentative plans at the moment, but I thought it would be useful to have these various possibilities before the House at this time.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE

speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker. If, indeed, it does seem useful to meet tomorrow to avoid coming back next week, the motion I would put forward would be for Friday hours with the exception of private members' business.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the government House leader has reported faithfully on the discussions which have taken place. I suggest that if we were to have further discussions later, we could well work things out. That, of course, remains to be seen. My main reason for rising at this point, however, is to indicate to the House, as I think I should, that when Bill C-52 is called there is one major point of order I shall be raising with respect to some of the proposed report stage amendments.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again we are aware of the urgency, for the House to adopt as soon as possible a procedure establishing a schedule of its business for a whole year.
There are certain things I cannot understand, Mr. Speaker; I felt that all members agree with this suggestion, but nothing is done. There are certain things with which we totally disagree, and still the House takes actions. At least we should be informed in advance of the procedures used for the matters on which we have total agreement, and I think it is normal to wonder about the length of sessions and the adjournment dates to enable families to get together, particularly at Christmas. As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, I have quite a large family and I would like to see them. It is the only opportunity I have during the year and I think it is the same with the others too.
Mr. Speaker, I therefore fully agree that we should sit tomorrow to avoid travelling uselessly. And if we can adjourn tomorrow night, I shall have the impression that I have contributed to give all my colleagues the opportunity to go back home and do things that are very personal during the days which precede Christmas. I dare say everybody understands.

subtopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT AND CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION ACT AUTHORIZATION FOR CMHC TO MAKE INTEREST REDUCTION GRANTS, CASH GRANTS, ETC., TO ENCOURAGE HOUSE CONSTRUCTION

speechtext: The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-77, to amend the National Housing Act and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act, as reported (without amendment) from the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

subtopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT AND CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION ACT AUTHORIZATION FOR CMHC TO MAKE INTEREST REDUCTION GRANTS, CASH GRANTS, ETC., TO ENCOURAGE HOUSE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
That Bill C-77, an act to amend the National Housing Act and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act, be amended in clause 1 by striking out lines 4 to 6 at page 2 and substituting the following therefor:
"(a) the rentals to be charged by the owner of the rental housing project shall be established by the corporation and that in so establishing and reviewing such rentals the corporation shall have regard for the probable family income of the lessees of each family housing unit;"
He said: Mr. Speaker, the amendment I have moved on behalf of our party is very important and crucial in order to help solve the serious housing crisis we have in Canada today. I am sure all of us would agree that the serious housing problem is really in three areas: supply, interest rates, and price. The solution the minister has adopted with regard to these problems is through the Assisted Home Ownership Program by the use of subsidies. He hopes to solve the problems of high interest rates and price by giving subsidies to a certain group in the country so that they may be better able to buy homes. May I point out to the minister and to members of the House that the subsidy approach to AHOP will not solve the serious housing problems we have today; it will not solve the problem of supply, interest rates or price, and in fact will be of very little significance with regard to these three main problems.
The reason it will not help the problem of supply is that the land is in the control of the builders and developers who may release it at at a time appropriate to them when they can make the highest possible profit. With respect to interest rates, the minister and the president of CMHC have told us that there will be no decline in interest rates in 1976. Probably the prevailing rate of 12 per cent will apply through 1976 and will afford no protection or help to people who buy homes. With regard to price, we have seen a significant increase in the price of homes right across the country. In the city of Toronto the average retail price of a home is now $69,600, and the average price across the countrv has increased from approximately $41,000 to $45,000.
We do not believe that the subsidy approach to AHOP will solve the difficult problems we have. In fact, if you look at the housing situation in Ontario and consider the $500 first home owner grant that the minister provided up to the end of October to assist purchasers, and the $1,500 grant given by the government of Ontario to stimulate
National Housing Act
house purchases, you will find in any serious study that the total grant of $2,000 just increases the price of homes in Ontario by that amount. The best evidence we have is the limits the minister released as proposed under the AHOP program. This year, in Toronto, the rate was $43,000. The new rate that the minister proposes is $47,000, an increase of 9 per cent. I could go across the country using the minister's table to show that the price with regard to AHOP purchases must be increased so that the program can be of advantage. In Montreal, the price has to be increased from $29,000 to $31,500. In Ottawa-Hull, the price has to be increased from $35,000 to $38,000. In Winnipeg, from $33,000 to $35,600; in Lethbridge from $28,000 to $31,000; in Prince George, from $37,000 to $39,000; and in Yellowknife, from $39,500 to $43,500.
In other words, for the minister to make the AHOP program work under his subsidies, the price limits have to be raised in various regions across the country. I do not think that proposal attacks the high prices that we have. We in the New Democratic Party say that the problem of housing has to be attacked in three main areas. First, with regard to the cost of land; second, with regard to high interest rates; and third, an increase in public housing. We see no evidence that the minister is acting to bring down the high cost of land. In fact, if anything, the price of land will increase in the coming year. I have already said that the prevailing interest rate of 12 per cent will obtain during 1976. If you were to follow HUDAC, the interest rate would go to 123/i per cent or 13 per cent, which would afford no help to the average person.
I have said that the third objective is to increase public housing. The minister has travelled through Europe and has seen the great strides they have made in public housing. I have done the same. In the early part of this year I was in Sweden. I spoke to the chief government architect, who told me of the serious problem they had and the approach they took. That was to tremendously increase public housing, and they now have sufficient. I saw some buildings with three and four vacant apartments, which contrasts to the low vacancy rate we have across this country. I am sure the parliamentary secretary and the minister will agree that the vacancy rate is 1.2 per cent, so this is a very serious problem.
This indicates the necessity of increasing the amount of public housing. I have pointed out to the minister that in the CMHC budget of 1972 the allocation to public housing was 37.3 per cent, and in 1974 it dropped to 19.2 per cent. This indicates that the minister had downgraded public housing in the total housing picture. He has promised me that there will be a significant increase in the 1976-77 budget for CMHC. Mr. Speaker, I have no faith in this government increasing the allocation with regard to public housing. After hearing the speech on restraint last night that put the burden on the ordinary and poor people in this country, I am sure that when the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) presents his budget to the government they will apply the same type of restraint which they indicated last night and there will be very little change in the moneys allocated to public housing.
This is why we in the New Democratic Party want action with regard to public housing. This is why we have brought forward this amendment to help people in respect

December 19, 1975
National Housing Act
of public housing. I should like to read the amendment, Mr. Speaker, and indicate the essential part of it. It reads:
(a) the rentals to be charged by the owner of the rental housing project shall be established by the corporation and that in so establishing and reviewing such rentals the corporation shall have regard for the probable family income of the lessees of each family housing unit.
With regard to the minister's approach on private limited dividend housing, he has made a major shift in philosophy. Prior to Bill C-77, the formula for rents of private limited dividend housing took into account the family income of the tenants. The minister has now completely abandoned that principle and has left it to the developer and builder to determine; he has completely ignored the family income of the tenants. The minister and CMHC have had a particular experience with regard to determining rents in public housing projects and public limited dividend projects. It is the government that determines the rents. Two factors determine rents in such projects: cost and, more importantly, the tenant's family income. It is possible, by using this method, to work out a tenant's rent quickly and efficiently.
What has the minister done, Mr. Speaker? He has abandoned this approach to private limited dividend housing and will depend on the builder to determine rents. He is telling the builder, in so many words, to ignore totally the family income of tenants in a project, saying that the cost to the builder shall determine rent and family income is to be ignored. I cannot understand why the minister took this approach. I suppose he feels he must do it to stimulate private limited dividend housing. But should this be done by giving builders and developers subsidies and letting them determine rents on the basis of cost?

speechtext: The House resumed, from Thursday, December 18, consideration of Bill C-69, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before we were interrupted last night for the evening performance which has since been variously described as a "con game" or a "shell game", I was dealing with the clause in the Unemployment Insurance Act amendments having to do with alteration of the bench mark. I would be happier to accept the arguments put forward by government spokesmen in this connection if the government had made certain changes in the act designed to make it more truly an insurance plan.
I should like to put on record the results of an analysis showing how payments were disbursed in 1974. It really turns out to be a gigantic transfer system from one part of the country to another. Benefit payouts in 1974 amounted to approximately $2,100 million-if costs of administration are added, the total figure comes to approximately $2,300 million. Approximately $1,600 million was raised by employee-employer deductions, leaving some $700 million to be drawn from the federal treasury. This works out, on the basis of an even tax adjustment, to approximately $30 million for every million people.
Some comparisons showing the extent to which each province benefited are interesting. Newfoundland contributed something like $50 million in employee-employer premiums, and received $114 million in benefit payments to its unemployed. New Brunswick paid approximately $55 million, and received $105 million by way of benefits. Quebec's share amounted to approximately $580 million in payments, while its citizens received $740 million in benefits. Ontario costs to employers and employees are estimated at $900 million; its citizens received $600 million in benefit pay-outs. Relative to their population, the three prairie provinces fared the worst. Manitoba contributed approximately $100 million, and received $50 million in return; Saskatchewan contributed something like $70 million, and received $46 million or so in return; Alberta fared the worst per population, contributing somewhere in the neighbourhood of $170 million and receiving $66 million. I estimate that in British Columbia the amounts paid and the amounts received were approximately the same.
December 19, 1975

An interesting article appeared in the Globe and Mail of December 11 under the heading "Regional unemployment disparities remain at surprisingly constant levels". This study, by Arthur Donner and Fred Lazar, showed that unemployment figures in the various parts of Canada have varied remarkably little over the years, unemployment being persistently low on the prairies and high in the Atlantic provinces. The authors ascribe this state of affairs to two main reasons. The first is that in Quebec and the maritime region there is a high rate of job transfer. They suggest that if regional job turnover differences were eliminated, the unemployment rates in the three high unemployment regions would be relatively lower, ranging anywhere from zero to 20 per cent above Ontario's rate. Further according to the authors of this article it is probable that the highly seasonal nature of employment and job opportunities in the three areas of high unemployment are the cause of this situation.
In my view, this calls attention to a weakness in the plan. A seasonal worker employed for 20 weeks of the year is often as well off financially as one who works for 50 weeks of the year. The present unemployment insurance system is deficient inasmuch as it fails to take into account a worker's total earnings for the year. It also fails to take account of the situation in the prairie provinces, for example, where large numbers of the population are selfemployed and contribute heavily to the fund through the general tax structure without the possibility of benefiting directly since self-employed people cannot claim unemployment insurance.
The survey may also indicate that administrators in rural communities are able to keep off the rolls many would-be recipients by strict use of the regulations. Indeed, it might fairly be said that many workers in rural areas have little chance of drawing benefits under the regulations the commission is presently following. The people affected are very often casual workers. These people are usually in the lower income brackets, working at jobs which, by and large, others do not want-for example, the farm housewife who goes to cook at logging or construction camps. She would be ruled out under the residence rule. She must pay unemployment insurance but has little or no chance of ever obtaining benefits; and, of course, she must contribute to the general tax structure.
I also ask whether the enormous transfer of funds from one area of the country to another to maintain the unemployed is the best method of using our money power. Certainly, if a worker lives in a high unemployment area he is likely to be able to obtain, if he wishes, enough money from short-time work to tide him over the year. It is not hard to obtain work at the average weekly wage in various parts of the country at some time of the year, even if a person has to move out of his home area. For workers who wish to take advantage of this, it seems that there are many built-in disadvantages to moving from an area of relatively high unemployment to an area where the work would be less seasonal and steadier.
The introduction of increased employee-employer deductions, with the raising of the benchmark, might be an improvement if true insurance principles were followed. But these few amendments to the Unemployment Insur-
Unemployment Insurance Act
ance Act are not likely to be very effective. I suggest that we have to take a look at the eight to 16 weeks' employment provision and at whether it is not too generous. If a person is only able to work eight weeks a year, surely he needs assistance other than unemployment insurance. There must be some serious impediment to his finding a job.
In addition, there should be more supervision of seasonal workers in the sense that some effort is made to assess their total working hours and income. It is well known that many companies carry the so-called black book, whereby workers can bank hours and these are taken up when they are laid off in the wintertime. More recognition must also be given the lower paid workers who contribute to unemployment insurance week in and week out and who are never unemployed, so therefore never make use of the system. They still pay their premiums and taxes. Many of these people harbour a great feeling of disillusionment because they feel they are victims of the system. I think the system would be more acceptable and workable if those who are unemployed were given either a bonus or paid lower premiums.

Mr. Speaker, I debated with myself whether I should say anything on this particular amendment before the House, but after listening to the announcements made yesterday and last night I decided it was only appropriate that I make a few remarks. There are two matters that occurred to me arising from the events of yesterday, and they have direct relevance to the bill before the House. I am glad this bill has been examined as thoroughly as it has for the last five days, which permitted the announcements of last night and yesterday afternoon to be made. It tends to put things into proper perspective as far as the members of this party and many people in the country are concerned. This is why I am glad the bill is under scrutiny at this moment.
The two events that occurred yesterday rather intrigued me. The first was the announcement in the afternoon of the surtax by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). One of the fascinating things about the announcement was that for a person earning $35,000 a year with two children, the surtax would amount to $10. That is the kind of restraint I like to see. I really enjoy it because it is an illustration of the problem we are facing. Then we had the announcement last night.
I should like to say something about the comments that floated across the House in regard to this clause. We were told by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) that we have to remove the disincentives from the Unemployment Insurance Act, and perhaps, in effect, this is what the minister has done. But I am always amazed at this business of disincentives and incentives. Why is it that we can take $10 surtax from someone earning $35,000 a year, but cannot take more because we do not want to kill his incentive to work, whereas when you give a hand-out to the poor people it is called a disincentive to work. I do not understand that sort of concept.

speechtext:
If the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) would give as much time to making a speech on the bill, we in the House would appreciate it. Clause 22, which we are trying to amend, changes the benchmark beyond which the government will pick up any deficits in the unemployment insurance fund. We refuse to accept this clause as being relevant at this time. When the act was brought into being in 1971, the benchmark was set at 4 per cent. At that time the minister's predecessor argued that the benchmark ought to be 4 per cent because that was a high enough rate of unemployment and would always act as an incentive to the government to keep the unemployment rate down. That sounded like a very plausible argument at the time, that it was an incentive for the government to keep unemployment below 4 per cent. Now we are to have a disincentive.
Obviously, that figure has not incited the government to do anything to bring down unemployment. How callous is a government that sets out to fight inflation by creating unemployment, by telling the people of Canada that the government would like to keep the unemployment rate below 4 per cent in order to keep the rate down? It did not work then, so the government is proposing to change the benchmark to the average of the previous eight years' unemployment rate. In January, 1976 this will mean an effective rate of 5.6 per cent. If the present rate of unemployment goes up, by 1977 it will be 6 per cent.
What, exactly, is the government doing? It is escaping responsibility that it ought to face. It is redefining unemployment. Each time the government had to go to general revenue for money, it held up its policies to examination by the taxpayers of Canada. It will now escape this responsibility. Nothing the government has done since 1971 indicates to us that it is prepared to come to grips with unemployment. In the committee we were told that 894,000 people collect unemployment insurance. That is a scandalous record for a government which from 1968 to the present time has enjoyed a majority. It just answers for the mistakes it has made and its faulty decisions in running this country. Now it wants to redefine the whole issue of unemployment and therefore escape its responsibility. That is the primary reason we are opposing this.
By redefining the rate of unemployment, the government, in effect, is saying that the employers and employees will have to pick up what normally the government would have paid out of the general revenue of this country which was collected on a progressive income tax basis. The present system, of course, is nothing but a regressive form of taxation. It means that those who are working and the small employers will have to pick up the deficit in the fund. In effect, the government is making these people pay for its mistakes and its bad policies of the past. Who are the people who will have to pay? As you may know, Mr. Speaker, the Unemployment Insurance Commission only insures up to a maximum of $8,500. So in effect because most of the working people in this country earn below that

figure they are the ones who will pick up the bulk of the deficit which the government is shifting to their shoulders.
I mentioned earlier the restraint being shown by this government and how it has chosen to fight inflation. We have been told by the government that it has chosen to fight inflation, and we have been given examples. The first example is how tough it intends to be with the high income earners, the $35,000-a year boys. Then we were told about the elimination of the dependency rate in this act. Then there is the matter of family allowances. Last night we heard what they are doing about that. The government is removing the indexing of family allowances. So, while they are patting themselves on the back for having improved the social programs, on the other hand another minister says that they have been too generous and therefore this will have to be cut off because of the fact the programs have been improved. This is the kind of double-talk that creates cynicism among the workers of the country. The policy of the government seems to be that it must make an example of the working people and carry on the fight on their backs. The move to change the benchmark is another example.
Let us look at another example of how we are to fight inflation in this House. We are told that members of parliament will not have an increase in wages, but that does not include the tax-free allowance. It might have been better had this applied to the tax-free allowance because the government would have received 40 per cent from that. This "now you see it, now you don't" policy amounts to nothing more than an attempt to fight inflation on the backs of the poor people by telling them that they must economize in the cause of the fight against inflation while at the same time the government makes no attempt to improve its policies. There is no attempt to establish a full employment policy. While the government to the south is considering a full employment policy, this government does not try to come to grips with it.
We are told we must produce more, as if we do not have the capability to produce more. We are operating on only 80 per cent or 82 per cent of our productive capacity. We have 18 per cent of our productive capacity lying idle in terms of 700,000 people unemployed. Surely, with the expertise and experience the government has, it should not be too difficult for it to improve productivity in this country and bring down inflation. The government, however, will not do that. That is not its purpose.
We in this party are not the only ones who oppose the change in the benchmark. The Canadian Labour Congress has opposed the increase in the benchmark for a very good reason. Again, it is the low income earners who will bear the burden. The result of the increase in the premiums will be something in the. order of 35 per cent to 40 per cent. These increases will bfl'h.orne by the bulk of the working class people in this country who earn $8,500. Those who have incomes above that, those earning $20,000, $30,000, and so on, will get away with the maximum which will be the same as anyone with an income of $8,500 will have to pay in respect of unemployment insurance premiums. This is very unfair. There is nothing progressive about it.
At least under the old system we could hold the government accountable for the hundreds of millions of dollars transferred from general revenue to the unemployment

insurance fund to make up the deficit. Even the progressive items in this bill are not to become effective immediately. They will become effective somewhere in the future. Even those things which are advantageous to the working class people will become a reality on January 1, 1976, but this regressive clause is to become effective on January 1, 1976. If I had my way, we would remain here until January 1, 1976, in order to prevent this clause going through, because it is not fair when we consider the actions of the government over the past and in the last few days in respect of justice concerning any programs.
We on this side of the House in this party, as I have said, are not the only ones who oppose the change in the benchmark. I pointed out that the Canadian Labour Congress opposes it because it is a hidden tax which increases the premiums of the working people between 35 per cent and 40 per cent, while the wealthy get away with a 10 per cent surtax. This is a travesty of justice. The Canadian Council on Social Development also opposes this. That council is much closer to the problems of the working poor than is anyone in this House.
This government has not attempted to do anything about the elimination of regional disparity in this country, the same disparity the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) referred to in 1968 when he said there were two things the government would do. The Prime Minister said that the government would create national unity and would eliminate regional disparities. We are no closer to national unity, and nothing has been done about regional disparity. In my area the unemployment rate is 10 per cent. In the riding to the west, Algoma, it is 20 per cent. We have not seen any policy that is directed toward creating more employment in areas such as northern Ontario, the Atlantic provinces and the northern parts of some of the other provinces.
It is interesting to note that all the government can do is throw out terminal programs such as LIP and OFY at the first signs of trouble. The first programs they cut are LIP and OFY, so everyone pats them on the back and they say they always knew the programs were a rip-off.
Here we see a direct attempt to distract the attention of the Canadian people from the real problem, which is, of course, that this government has not attempted to establish any program to create employment. That is why we have such a drain on unemployment insurance. We have said the contrary, that the Unemployment Insurance Act has been an incentive for persons to improve their status in the work force. It has given them flexibility and mobility and it has been a way of making employers improve the working conditions in their plants. It has forced them to improve wage rates and it has been an incentive, in many instances, to improve working conditions and the rate of pay in this country.
What do we find the minister is doing in this bill? We say it is a regressive move because, as I have said before, it avoids facing the issue fairly and squarely. Every year the unemployment rate will be redefined and they will shift more and more of the cost on to the working poor. That is dishonest. At least the other way around they have to come to the committee studying the estimates and justify why they are transferring so many hundreds of millions of
Unemployment Insurance Act
dollars. That way they are put under the scrutiny of the public, of the press and of members of parliament. They could not stand the heat of that kind of scrutiny, so they cooked up this little scheme, probably hatched by their nabobs to get them off the hook, off the griddle. All they have to do is, poof, one amendment, thus redefining the whole issue of what full employment is in this country. But they cannot do that. The problem will not go away. You have to have a pretty big rug to hide things under.
The fact of the matter is that certainly the economy will suffer when there are over 894,000 people unemployed and 700,000 of them collecting unemployment insurance. To me one of the greatest travesties that this House has seen in a long time is to have so many people living off the unemployment insurance fund. To accuse people of ripping off unemployment insurance is to avoid facing the facts. The fact of the matter is that they have embarked on a program which will only exacerbate unemployment in this country rather than create employment.
It seems to me that we have said the poor will be picking up the cost. Certainly the working poor will be picking up the cost, but the poor have no way of passing on that cost because now, with the Anti-Inflation Board in place, a worker is limited with respect to the percentage increase he can have. The employer, on the other hand, if his premiums are increased as a result of a clause in this bill, has a way of getting it back. He can increase the cost of his product. Of course, the Anti-Inflation Board gives him the possibility to do that because it permits the pass-through cost, so he can increase the cost of his product and of course he will. Any entrepreneur will do that. That is why we say that the workers are locked in. They have a government which is prepared to block them from passing on their expenses, but on the other hand employers are quite free to pass on any increased cost to the customers, to the consumers and to the workers. We oppose this clause. We consider it to be retrograde.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
That is the question. This clause of the bill is very important. It takes me back a number of years to the time when we previously discussed the Unemployment Insurance Act and the attitude of the Liberal party regarding their contribution as a government to unemployment. I can remember sitting on a committee together with the Hon. Paul Martin who kept insisting that the Liberal government of the day had always provided money when unemployment became the responsibility of the government.
At that time, the Conservatives were in government and they were resisting the idea of the government putting any money into unemployment insurance. It is interesting to note that the Conservative party continues to feel that way, and so do the Liberal party members, who have always said they were willing to make a contribution when unemployment rose above the normal insurable level.

December 19, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
When the Hon. Paul Martin made clear the stand of his party with regard to unemployment, he said he would go to his office and come back with the exact information. On his return, he informed us about the contribution that had been made by his party on two occasions. We learned it amounted to less than $400,000. If you remember, the talk at that time was that we were heading into a major recession in 1959-1961, but yet that was the contribution which he indicated had been in keeping with the Liberal party's philosophy.
I am of the opinion that the workers of this country can only be guaranteed an insurance program up to a point. I want to note that the exercise we were put through yesterday on the matter of constraints was not at the request of the workers of this country, but because the government wants to handle a totally different problem. In doing that, they will find there will be a fall-out, no matter how big or small it is, which will result in unemployment in this country. When the government takes action which results in unemployment, the worker cannot be guaranteed an insurance against that type of unemployment.
Initially, when we spoke about the level at which the government should put in some money to cover the action they are taking, we spoke about 2 per cent as being the normally expected unemployment rate. The next time the Unemployment Insurance Act was before us, 4 per cent was considered as the normal unemployment rate. Now they have got it up to 5.6 per cent. I suggest that if we look ahead another ten years we might find a 10 per cent, 11 per cent or 12 per cent unemployment rate considered as normal. If that is to be the normal rate, then it seems to me that the workers might as well stop making any attempt to obtain an insurance program against unemployment.
There will come a time, if it has not already arrived, when the workers will not be able to pay the premium and we will find ourselves in exactly the same position as the farmers who are asked to pay insurance to protect themselves against loss of income, crops or against other disasters. They have arrived at a point at which it is not to their advantage to pay the premium because it is too high and because the return will be too small on it. For the working people to insure themselves against unemployment, which we consider to be normally 5 per cent, is a heavy load to be carrying because it applies in the main to people who are making less than $8,500 a year. They will take advantage of it, and they are paying too high a price in the middle.
Surely everyone agrees that if the government takes action which results in producing unemployment, the government should be responsible. We should be responsible collectively. We cannot expect the worker to make the premium payments when we are proposing, in effect, a solution to another problem altogether. That does not seem to be the kind of insurance workers should be asked to carry.
I am sure some hon. members will say that the worker is not being asked to carry it all; part of the cost is being paid by the employer. Anyone who says that knows nothing about the negotiations which take place between an employer and his employee. When an employee talks to his boss about wages, the whole cost factor of his labour is

taken into consideration. If he does not benefit in one way, he may benefit in another. However, if an employee does not enjoy fringe benefits, some of which are considered to be unemployment insurance compensation, vacation pay and other benefits, he may receive benefits by way of wages. In any case, it is a worker's wage package we are talking about, not a cost to an employer or to the government. The government has said it will give up its responsibility for situations it creates and we are going to have a sliding scale, so that it will continue to go up and the government will not have to worry about it.
Along with the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), I was happy to see the government share in the responsibility for unemployment. Perhaps other hon. members were not. Not only does the worker carry the unemployed by way of his contributions, but over a certain level the government has to carry its responsibility. I believe the rate should have stayed at 2 per cent, but it became 4 per cent. The government cannot stand the heat of unemployment at 4 per cent. It now wants to raise the rate to something over 5 per cent and this winter it may well reach a rate of 6 per cent for which the Unemployment Insurance Act is supposed to be responsible.
Premiums will be so high that there will be a violent revolution on the part of the employed against carrying that insurance rate for the unemployed. It is very hard for an individual who is paying high unemployment insurance premiums to realize that, but for the<grace of God, it may be him drawing the benefits, and I am sure he often fails to see the relationship. It seems to me that all hon. members should be concerned that we are taking away the responsibility of the government for providing full employment or employment at as high a rate as it is possible to maintain.
What the government did yesterday was create a situation whereby it will carry on most of the fight against inflation on the backs of the poor, and where changes have been made in this legislation those changes will be detrimental to the poor element in our employment structure. It will apply to the lower income group, and it has been said it will apply to only 5 per cent or 10 per cent of the labour force. It will, and no matter what the level will be, the people at the lower end of the scale will be least able to take any loss.
This government has had a chequered record with regard to unemployment insurance. Much contradictory philosophy has gone into the thinking of the Liberal party since unemployment insurance was initially a request by J. S. Woodsworth in exchange for his support in keeping the King government in power 40 years ago. The thinking of the government has been as tortured since that period of time as it has been in any other philosophical field of which I can think.
If the government wants to get rid of unemployment insurance, it should at least allow workers some time to study another kind of program which will supply them with income support which will be sufficient. There are many workers in this country who would totally change the program, but this government wants to operate the plan and wants to make the changes it is making. The minister can talk about the role of the government in relation to the Canada Pension Plan, to old age pensions and to provincial assistance in such things as medicare,
December 19, 1975

supplementary benefits and other social aspects, but as long as the government wants to relate these things together in its social structure it must assume some responsibility for making contributions when actions it takes in other fields are detrimental to the employment picture in the nation.
Those hon. members who really want to see an unemployment insurance program continue should consider very carefully allowing the government to make the change it is contemplating in the benchmark, and taking away from the government the responsibility of coming as close as it believes possible to providing full employment and assuming responsibility above that amount. Ten years ago 2 per cent was bad, and 4 per cent in 1971 was considered a national responsibility. Anything up to 5.2 per cent presently appears to be satisfactory to this minister. By spring, that rate will probably be 6 per cent. I believe the government has a responsibility. I think, by this amendment, the government would be exercising that responsibility by reinstating the 4 per cent ceiling, which I would consider to be at least double an acceptable figure in a country with our resources if it were operated by a government which provided good economic leadership.

Mr. Speaker, I was saying that nothing is more cynical than clause 38. Clause 38(2) clearly defines those clauses of the legislation which will come into effect on January 1, 1976. What are those clauses? They are clauses 1(2), 10, 22 and 31. These are the clauses which eliminate the 65-year olds from coverage under the Unemployment Insurance Act, and which change the bench mark that in effect re-defines what the government considers to be full employment.
What we are attempting in this amendment is to include also in that effective date of January 1, 1976, those clauses which add some manner of progressiveness to the Unemployment Insurance Act. The first of those is the extension of the qualifying period. We are in agreement with that. We feel that in respect of those who have been sick, or in some way disabled, this is a progressive clause which would extend the qualifying period so that they could go back two years to the time before they were so disabled or so taken sick. There was even a private member's bill from this side of the House in the name of the hon. member for Nickel Belt which would extend the qualifying period. So we admit this is a progressive move and feel that surely it should come into effect on January 1, 1976.
The other clause which we feel should come into effect on January 1, 1976, is the clause in respect of voluntary termination of a claim, which we believe is a progressive step. As we know there is no provision in the act for voluntary termination of a claim. It seems to me that clause 14 would provide this kind of a progressive move. It is a move that is long overdue. It should have been included in the act when it was brought in in 1971.
We also feel that clause 31 is a progressive move and that this clause should be included in the provisions of clause 38(2). This clause, which would provide for the payment of expenses of anyone appearing before the umpire, we believe is long overdue. Indeed we found out during the committee hearings that there were 40,000 appeals to the board of referees. In that same period only 400 appeals were made to the umpire. In other words one per cent of the appeals to the referees ended up as appeals to the umpire.
Certainly there must be a reason for such a low number of appeals going to the umpire. We suspect what the reason is. The minister has promised that a study is under way of the appeal procedures. One reason we do not think this section has been working to the advantage of the claimants is the fact that many of the claimants must travel long distances in order to appear before the umpire. We think that has been a disincentive to claimants. Therefore we
December 19, 1975

believe clause 31 is a progressive step since it will provide for payment of expenses of those claimants who must travel some distance in order to appear before the umpire.
What do we find in clause 38? The cynicism is paramount. We find that the regressive steps which eliminate the 65-year olds from unemployment insurance, and which change the bench mark the government is prepared to make effective January 1, 1976.
When we asked the minister the reason why these other progressive steps could not be made effective the same date, January 1, 1976, he gave a phony answer. The minister said that these adjustments cannot be put into effect because it is administratively difficult. What is administratively difficult about paying the expenses of the claimants who appear before the umpire? It should not be difficult administratively to do this, with all the computers that are available to the government. The Unemployment Insurance Commission uses a computer very extensively. As a matter of fact the officials use it so extensively that when there is a problem concerning claimants the answer is that it was the computer which made the mistake. The government also has available to it the highly paid nabobs in the administration.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: What is a nabob?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
A nabob is someone hired by the Unemployment Insurance Commission to give the government advice. The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) says they are one step above a mandarin. Perhaps they are baby mandarins.
With all these high paid mandarins, nabobs, and flunkeys in the Unemployment Insurance Commission they cannot tell us that they cannot come up with a plan to get around the administrative hang-ups to make the progressive aspects of the minister's proposals effective on the same day on which the negative aspects will become effective. I suppose this would tax their brains, but I suspect that it will not tax their abilities.
I suspect that it is a deliberate attempt by the minister to say, "Look how tough I am". Look how tough he is with those who are collecting unemployment insurance and how tough he is with the poor, when we know that 70 per cent of those collecting unemployment insurance earn under $6,000! He is a pretty big and a pretty tough man when it comes to dealing with the little people, but when it comes to taking on the big guys making $35,000 a year, all he wants from them is a surtax of $10. When it comes to taking on those who receive family allowances, he takes off indexing of family allowances. I suppose that very shortly the government will want a means test for those who collect family allowances. See how tough they are with the little people. When it comes to the big ones, they curl up and start purring like a big tabby cat. That is the way it works.
The minister says it is administratively difficult to put clause 31 into effect, the clause under which travel and other expenses are paid for those who wish to appear before the umpire. He says it would be administratively difficult to terminate a claim voluntarily. It would not be difficult because we know full well that, if it is administra-
Unemployment Insurance Act
tively easy to let the claim run on, they must have a process of knowing when a person establishes a claim which is continued. They have the computer set up; they know exactly when the claim is terminated so that a person who applies beyond that date is ineligible for unemployment insurance benefits. If they can set up a computer which tells them that a person who has collected maternity or sickness benefits after 29 weeks has terminated his or her claim, surely it should not be difficult for the government and this department to set up a computerized system which, on notification from the UIC in writing or by telephone, would immediately halt that claim.
I believe that a claimant should always have had the right to terminate the claim once he returned to work. But the government took that step in 1971. It was a discriminatory move, and now the minister leaves the change for some time in the future.
For us to accept this bill in the House at this point is very difficult because this is a regressive measure. We will not be serving the taxpayers and the people of Canada properly if we accept it under the present conditions.
The other clause which we think should become effective on January 1, 1976, is the extension of the qualifying period. Surely it should not be difficult to set up a system qualifying a person who has been jail, or on compensation, or who has been collecting a disability pension beyond one year. It should be possible to pick out his file and pick out the 104 weeks and see what earnings he has had within the 104 weeks. They are doing it now. They must have the latest separation certificate and they must look over the previous 52 weeks. It must be just as difficult administratively to look back at 52 weeks as it is to look back at 104 weeks. For them to say it is not, is just bullroar. I think the nabobs told them that that is one thing they do not want to put into effect now because of an ulterior motive, which is to build up the minister to look as if he were the greatest inflation fighter since Buckley. That is what they have attempted to do. They have tried to build him up as the greatest inflation fighter. It is easy to be a great inflation fighter when you are dealing with the little people, but when he is dealing with the big guys he pulls in his claws.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Let us have your Christmas present now.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Never fear, you will get it. We look to the minister as if he were Santa Claus, but in fact he is nothing but a big Scrooge. He gave them a Christmas present. What is the Christmas present he has given them? He has informed the 65 year olds that they will not be covered after January 1. What has he told people on family allowances who are poor and may be unemployed? He has told them that they will not get the indexing. He is giving them a New Year's present. Boy, he sure can hand out presents! In effect, he tells them that they will get these things, effective on January 1, 1976, but not the beneficial clauses. That is the quarrel we have with him.
Even at this stage of the game we are prepared to move an amendment which would include these beneficial clauses. All the minister has to do is to rise and say he is prepared to move for their inclusion in the bill and to let them come into effect on January 1, 1976. I would be the first one to sit down if he were prepared to stand up and

say that he is prepared to include the beneficial items in this bill.
There is no one in the House who would like to go home for Christmas more than I do. I would certainly like to go home tomorrow because I have five small children at home. But in no way can I in good conscience let the minister get away with this subterfuge. All he has to do now is to rise in his place-but he is not interested in doing that because he wants to chat with that chatterbox from the Maritimes. He is not prepared to bring in those beneficial clauses. I know that members on the other side are concerned about that. I am sure that they come from parts of the country much like mine where people have problems with unemployment insurance when they cannot voluntarily suspend their claims or extend the qualifying period. I am also sure they have problems with claimants who want to appeal to the umpire but cannot afford the travel expenses to reach the place where the umpire is holding court. We are remiss if we are not prepared to insist that the minister include the beneficial clauses in the bill.
We have tried to examine this bill as closely as possible, and we have made our concrete and positive proposals in committee and at report stage. Now we have come to the last clause in the bill, which is the crunch. We appeal to the minister to include these particular beneficial clauses in the bill so that at least the edge will be taken off the negative clauses in the bill. I can say no more than to call on the minister to do that, and to give the House some assurance that these measures will be brought in on January 1, 1976. He owes it to the people of Canada because the government, in effect, has been the cause of high unemployment in the country. Surely he should be the one to rise in the House to say that at least the beneficial and progressive items in the bill will come into effect on January 1, 1976.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: With regard to timing, the Bill C-69 provision which will become effective with Royal Assent is the insurability of LIP and LEAP individual sponsors, which is Clause 38(3).

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: You are cutting that out.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
No, we are not cutting out LIP. The hon. member for Nickel Belt is partly correct with regard to some of the clauses which will become effective-I want to be precise about this-on January 1 or January 4. There is still some problem about those two or three days because some of these affect the benefit cycle. The hon. member is correct about the increase in the period of disqualification, the dependency rate, the repeal of coverage of persons 65 years of age, and the repeal of the advance pay.

The voluntary termination of claims, however, will be effective on the same date, either January 1 or January 4. The new financing threshold will be in effect then. There are quite a few of what I call housekeeping amendments. One could choose which are beneficial and which will take effect then.
I wish to make reference to an amendment to the act which was contained in Bill C-16, that is, the flexibility in the payment of maternity benefits. It will be effective on February 1. I say to the hon. member that there is no plot in this; it simply is a problem of computer programming. That bill was given Royal Assent on July 30, and the computer programming, procedures, guidelines, and staff training were not completed in time to make that effective before February 1.1 regret that, but that is the problem.
The flexibility in the payment of sickness benefits, which is by proclamation, and the extension of the qualifying period, the 104 weeks, are going to take computer re-programming. We cannot authorize the commission to expend what is some money involved in that until Royal Assent, and I am not trying to bamboozle the hon. member. It is a practical problem. The officials think it may take a few months to do that. I can only say that I will be watching very closely and pressing them to bring this into effect as quickly as possible. Those are the facts as we see them now.

point of order to raise a question of procedure on this matter. I should, however, first put the motion. The motion under consideration will be motion No. 1 in the name of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien).
Mr. Chretien moves:
Motion No. 1.
That Bill C-52, to amend the Public Service Superannuation Act, the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act, the Defence Services Pension Continuation Act, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Superannuation Act, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Pension Continuation Act, the Diplomatic Service (Special) Superannuation Act, the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act, the Governor General's Retiring Annuity Act, the Judges Act, the Tax Review Board Act and the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act, be amended by adding after line 11 at page 2 the following new Clause:
"2.1 The definition "salary" in subsection 2(1) of the said Act is
repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"salary" means
(a)	as applied to the Public Service, the basic pay received by the person in respect of whom the expression is being applied for the performance of the regular duties of a position for the office exclusive of any amount received as allowances, special remuneration, payment for overtime or other compensation or as a gratuity unless that amount is deemed to be or to have been included in that person's basic pay pursuant to any regulation made under paragraph 32(1) (b.2); and
(b)	as applied to the regular force or the Force, the pay or pay and allowances, as the case may be, applicable in the case of that person as determined under the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act or the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Superannuation Act;"
